name: Cromwell's Rule
statement: Never assign a probability of exactly 0 or 1 to anything that is not logically certain.
meaning: In Bayesian reasoning, avoid being absolutely certain about any contingent, empirical claim. Leave at least a sliver of doubt — and a sliver of credence for the alternative — so that evidence can still move your beliefs. It is intellectual humility written as a rule about priors.
mechanism: By Bayes' theorem, the posterior is proportional to the prior times the likelihood. If your prior for a hypothesis is 0, the posterior stays 0 no matter how strong the evidence; if it is 1, it stays 1. A prior of 0 or 1 is a locked door that no observation can open — so a dogmatic prior makes you literally unpersuadable by data. The fix, in Lindley's words, is to leave a little probability for even the wildest possibility, so that a surprise can still update you rather than leave you unmoved.

examples.text: Someone who assigns probability 0 to 'I might be wrong about this' can never be corrected: Bayesian updating is mathematically inert against a 0 or 1 prior, so no accumulation of contrary evidence changes their mind.

Lindley's illustration: keep the prior that the moon is made of green cheese tiny — one in a million, say — rather than zero, so that if astronauts returned with cheese samples your belief could actually update instead of being frozen.
A forecaster who calls an outcome '100% certain' or 'impossible' cannot rationally revise when reality diverges; calibrated forecasting keeps its probabilities strictly between 0 and 1.

variants.name: 'Think it possible you may be mistaken'
variants.text: Cromwell's own line, used as a stand-alone maxim of epistemic humility — the plain-English version of the rule.

variants.name: The strengthened form
variants.text: A version that rewrites the probability axiom itself, from 0 ≤ Pr(A) ≤ 1 to 0 < Pr(A) < 1 for any proposition that is not logically true or false.

whyItMatters: It is the mathematical case for open-mindedness: certainty of 0 or 1 is not confidence but a refusal to learn, because it makes belief immune to evidence. In forecasting, science, and everyday judgement, keeping a sliver of doubt is what lets you be moved by facts.

working.text: for any empirical claim, hold a prior strictly between 0 and 1 — even a tiny margin keeps you able to update.
when you catch yourself calling something impossible or certain, ask whether any evidence could change your mind; if not, your prior is locked.
assign certainty only to what is logically or mathematically true or false — everything contingent stays in the open interval.

limits: It is a normative principle of Bayesian reasoning, not a law of nature or a theorem, and it explicitly exempts logical and mathematical certainties, which legitimately take probability 0 or 1. In some engineering or modelling contexts it is convenient and harmless to treat certain events as impossible or certain by definition; the rule is a caution against doing so for genuinely empirical claims, not a blanket ban. Its force is prescriptive — how you ought to set priors — rather than a claim about the world.
misreadings: It does not say you must be uncertain about everything, including logic and mathematics — those can be certain. It says do not close the door on contingent, empirical claims, because a prior of 0 or 1 makes you unteachable by evidence.
origin: Named by the statistician Dennis Lindley, who set it out in his work on Bayesian decision-making. The name honours Oliver Cromwell's 1650 letter to the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland: 'I beseech you, in the bowels of Christ, think it possible that you may be mistaken.'

sources.text: Lindley, D.V. Making Decisions / Understanding Uncertainty. — where Lindley names and states the rule.
